newsitem.title: USA: Consumer credit grew steadily in July.
newsitem.headline: Consumer credit grew steadily in July.

text.p: Consumers reached for their credit cards freely in July, boosting overall instalment buying by $7.7 billion, the Federal Reserve said Monday.
While borrowing to buy new cars trailed off sharply, so-called revolving, or credit card, debt shot up at a 19.4 percent annual rate -- the fastest since a 20 percent jump in April.
The $7.7 billion expansion in all types of instalment credit during July followed a sharply revised $6.7 billion increase in June that previously was reported as a stronger $8.3 billion surge.

Analysts said strong job growth has made consumers more willing to spend and raised questions as to whether the economy will slow soon enough in the second half to head off more interest rate rises by the Fed to cool inflation.

In one indicator of the economy's vigour at the start of the second half, the Labour Department said Friday that the unemployment rate dropped to 5.1 percent in August, the lowest level in nearly 7-1/2 years, as the economy created 250,000 jobs.
During July, credit card debt jumped $7.2 billion, at a 19.4 percent annual rate, more than triple June's $2.1 billion gain, or 5.7 percent annual rate.

"Consumers' debt burden is rising, but incomes are up, employment is up and confidence is up, so if you wouldn't borrow now, when would you?" said Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co.

July's consumer credit increase represented an 8 percent annual rate of advance in instalment credit, compared with 7 percent in June. July was the fourth month in a row in which total credit expanded at single-digit rates after climbing at 10 percent and higher a month from January through March.

Analysts said the economy's 5-1/2-year-long expansion since the last recession in 1990-91 has enabled consumers to buy the new cars and other costly hard goods they wanted like appliances that typically are paid for by instalment financing.
"There's no reason to think that people won't keep borrowing with employment as healthy as it is, but the big double-digit increases are behind us," Dederick said.

Auto sales slowed in July, and that showed up in the consumer credit figures. Growth in new-car loans slowed abruptly to a $1.9 billion increase at a 6.3 percent annual rate from a June rise of $5.6 billion at an 18.5 percent annual rate.
Recent reports from automakers point to a rebound in sales of cars and light trucks in August.

Other credit, a category that includes consumer bank loans but not home equity loans, decreased in July for a fourth straight month, falling $1.5 billion at a 5.1 percent annual rate. This credit category had declined by $900,000, at a 3.5 percent annual rate, in June.
